title: PSPO vs CSPO: Which Product Owner Certification?
dek: Get the PSPO I if you're self-funding: it costs about $200, needs no course, has a real exam, and never expires. Get the CSPO if your employer is paying and you want two days of guided training — but it costs far more and needs renewing every two years.

seo.metaTitle: PSPO vs CSPO: Which Product Owner Cert?
seo.metaDescription: PSPO vs CSPO compared on cost, course, exam and renewal — and which Product Owner certification fits you, self-funded or employer-paid.

sources.label: Scrum.org — Professional Scrum Product Owner I (PSPO I)
Scrum Alliance — Certified Scrum Product Owner (CSPO)

body.richText: If you've decided on product ownership, there are two mainstream certifications: the PSPO I from Scrum.org and the CSPO from the Scrum Alliance. They cover almost the same material, so the decision comes down to four practical things — cost, whether a course is mandatory, whether there's an exam, and whether it expires.

Quick answer: if you're paying yourself, the PSPO I is the better value — around $200, self-study allowed, and it never expires. If your employer is paying and you learn better in a live class, the CSPO is a fine choice. Very few people should pay for the CSPO out of their own pocket.

body.caption: PSPO I vs CSPO on the factors that decide it (2026; confirm current fees with each body).

body.text: The real difference: what you're buying

body.richText: This is where people get confused by the price gap. The two organizations sell different things. Scrum.org sells you an assessment — you prove you know the material however you learned it, and the $200 is purely the exam. The Scrum Alliance sells you a course, with the certificate as its outcome; you're paying for two days of a trainer's time, not for a test.

That explains everything else. The CSPO has no exam because the course is the qualification, which also makes it a weaker signal of knowledge. The PSPO I has a demanding 85% pass mark, which makes it a stronger signal — but gives you no teaching at all.

items: You're paying for it yourself and want the best value
You're comfortable self-studying from the Scrum Guide and free resources
You want a credential that never expires and never charges you again
You want the harder exam as evidence you actually know the material
Your employer is paying, which removes the cost objection entirely
You genuinely learn better with a live instructor and group exercises
You want the interaction and questions a two-day class allows
Your local job market specifically names Scrum Alliance credentials

body.richText: Don't assume the more expensive one is more respected. Both are widely recognized, and most job postings that ask for a Product Owner certification accept either. Paying three or four times more out of your own pocket buys you teaching, not extra credibility.

body.text: Does either one get you hired?

richText: On its own, no — and this matters more than the choice between them. Product Owner is a decision-making role, so employers want evidence of judgement, not just a certificate. The credential gets you past filters; your track record gets you the job. We set out the realistic route in

items.question: Is the PSPO or CSPO better?
items.answerRichText: Neither is better as a credential — both are widely recognized and most employers accept either. The PSPO I is far better value for self-funded learners (~$200, no course, never expires), while the CSPO suits people whose employer pays for the mandatory two-day course.

items.question: Does the CSPO have an exam?
items.answerRichText: No. The CSPO is awarded on completion of the mandatory two-day course, with no exam required. The PSPO I is the opposite: no course is required, but you must pass an assessment of 80 questions in 60 minutes with a score of at least 85%.

items.question: Does the PSPO expire?
answerRichText: No. The PSPO I never expires and has no renewal fee — you pay once. The CSPO must be renewed every two years, which requires continuing education and a fee. Over several years that difference adds up. See
